detract

dih-TRAKT · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To detract is to take away from the value, importance, or quality of something (usually used with from).

A hairline crack in the antique vase's glaze did nothing to detract from its beauty -- collectors still fought over it at auction.

Example

A light drizzle all afternoon did nothing to detract from the joy of the outdoor wedding; guests simply passed around umbrellas and kept dancing.

The drizzle was a minor flaw, but it didn't lower the overall value of the day -- it failed to detract from the celebration, which is exactly how the word is used.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

diminish: To diminish something is to make it smaller, weaker, or less impressive, acting on the thing directly -- you diminish the pain, the supply, the enthusiasm itself. Detract works at one remove and pairs with from: a flaw detracts from a painting's beauty by pulling value away from it.

lessen: To lessen something is to make it smaller in amount or degree, acting on it head-on -- you lessen a fever, a burden, a risk. Detract never works head-on: it pairs with from and pulls value away from a quality, the way one sour note detracts from a song.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

enhance: to improve the quality or value of something

boost: to increase or improve something

Where it sits · how sharply the value drops — reduce → detract → cheapen

reduce vs. detract: To reduce something's impact is the mildest way to say it went down a bit; detract is sharper and always aims at value -- a flaw that detracts actively takes away from how good the whole thing seems.

cheapen vs. detract: To cheapen something is to make it seem noticeably less valuable or dignified, a sharper decrease than detract.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — de-

Prefix — de-: away (Latin)

Root — tract

Root — tract: to draw, to pull (from Latin trahere, 'to draw,' whose past-participle stem is tract-)

Put it together

Put it together: Detract combines de- ("away") with tract ("to draw, to pull," from Latin trahere) -- literally "to pull away" from something's value, which is exactly what the word describes today.

Use the root in a new word: attract

Use the root in a new word: attract: Marisol built her whole science-fair project around what attracts lightning.

Root Check

Word Choice

Detract is almost always used with the word from -- something detracts from the value or quality of something else.
